BOSTON BUILDING ENERGY EXPLORER← Data & methods

Course deliverable 04

What this data can tell us

A reflection on evidence, uncertainty and responsible comparison.

A useful screening tool

This project turns a difficult disclosure workbook into a transparent first step for investigation. The most consequential work was defining record grain. Without deduplication, campus summaries and their members could be counted together and buildings with shared meters could receive misleading rankings. The analysis retains 5,034 non-campus records, including records with missing or questionable values, while eligibility rules select the reference population separately.

What the data supports

The disclosure supports descriptions of recorded energy intensity, reporting coverage and differences among buildings with similar primary uses and broad floor-area bands. It identifies 666 buildings above their eligible peer group's upper quartile. These are candidates for questions about meter boundaries, operations, occupancy and equipment. Missing inputs and explicit anomalies support a separate data-review workflow. The scenario lets a visitor understand the arithmetic size of a peer gap without treating it as a promised outcome.

What it cannot prove

A single disclosure release does not establish annual trends or policy effects. Correlation between building characteristics and energy intensity does not establish causal effects of equipment or energy measures. Operating hours, building age, occupancy, equipment efficiency, retrofit costs and energy prices are unavailable or insufficient for causal or investment analysis. Even within the same property type and size band, operational differences and mixed uses remain. High EUI alone does not demonstrate poor management.

Uncertainty remains visible

Missingness, reporting quality and sample selection affect interpretation. Eligible buildings may systematically differ from excluded ones. A minimum of 20 peers avoids the smallest comparison groups but does not establish representativeness or statistical significance. Estimated emissions do not establish final emissions compliance, particularly where renewable-energy treatment, custom emissions factors and flexibility measures are absent. A peer-benchmark scenario is not an engineering savings estimate and cannot justify claimed emissions reductions, financial returns or payback.

What should happen next

For a selected energy candidate, verify the floor area and meter boundary, request operating schedules and occupancy information, and then consider an engineering assessment. For a review case, reconcile the original submission before interpreting its rank. A future evaluation of trends or policy would require harmonized multiple-year data and a credible comparison design. This release's energy-use year still needs explicit confirmation from the publisher. The practical contribution is a reproducible, inspectable decision aid with visible uncertainty.

Sources: Analyze Boston disclosure resource; Boston BERDO reporting and publication guidance. The supplied workbook and its Data Dictionary are the analytical source.
